title: Why PyTorch Is Used
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of why pytorch is used in a PyTorch workflow.
Apply a small example of why pytorch is used and interpret the output.
Identify a relevant limitation, debugging check, or reproducibility concern.

content.intro: Why PyTorch Is Used: PyTorch is a Python framework for tensor computation and neural-network workflows. A tensor is a typed, shaped collection of values; operators build computations from those values. In this lesson, use a small example to make the inputs, outputs, and boundary conditions explicit.
content.why_it_matters: A shared tensor model makes it possible to progress from simple numerical operations to differentiable models without switching the basic data abstraction. For this lesson, focus on tensor computation and automatic differentiation and the evidence you can collect from a controlled example.

content_blocks.text: A PyTorch workflow combines tensors and operators with autograd, neural-network modules, optimizers, and data-loading utilities. The source topics for this lesson are: Tensor computation and automatic differentiation, Neural-network development, GPU acceleration. Keep each topic connected to a checkable input/output behavior.

content_blocks.title: Read the example
content_blocks.text: Read the values and printed result first, then inspect how the operation transforms every tensor element. This tiny example is the foundation for later model code. The example is a teaching-scale check, not evidence of a trained model score or a hardware-independent performance claim.

content.task: Try it yourself: Create two small tensors, apply one element-wise operation and one reduction, then describe the output shape and value. Record the observed result and one limitation; do not report an unrun training or performance result as measured.
task_acceptance_criteria: The experiment demonstrates at least one relevant aspect of why pytorch is used.
Record the expected and observed result, including shape/dtype/device information when relevant.
Explain one common failure mode, compatibility limitation, or evaluation caveat.

troubleshooting.symptom: A tensor operation raises a shape, dtype, or device mismatch.
troubleshooting.check: Print .shape, .dtype, and .device for each input. Resolve the mismatch intentionally instead of changing dimensions blindly.

troubleshooting.symptom: The example fails because an optional package or accelerator is unavailable.
troubleshooting.check: Check the installed PyTorch/package versions and device availability. Use the official installation selector and run the CPU-compatible path where appropriate.

troubleshooting.symptom: The result differs across runs or machines.
troubleshooting.check: Fix the seed where useful, record versions and inputs, and document operations that remain nondeterministic or hardware dependent.

common_mistakes.problem: Relying on assumptions instead of inspecting the data or output.
common_mistakes.why: Many ML failures come from incorrect shapes, labels, preprocessing, or execution mode rather than a syntax error.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect representative inputs and add assertions for the expected shape, dtype, range, or behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing training-time behavior with inference-time behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Dropout, normalization, gradient tracking, and optimizer updates can change how a model behaves.
common_mistakes.fix: Do not assume that importing torch proves a model is correct; inspect actual tensor values and shapes.

common_mistakes.problem: Using a current or experimental API without recording its version assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Hardware support and ecosystem APIs can change independently of the core package.
common_mistakes.fix: Pin compatible dependencies, record the environment, and test after upgrades.
